passages.title: Questions 112 to 117
passages.attribution: The passage is shortened in our copy of the paper.
passages.text:
The expression 'the rule of law' relates to human association. It purports to stand for human beings associated in terms of the recognition of certain conditions of association, namely 'laws'; human beings joined in an exclusive, specifiable mode of relationship...

In short, while persons may have (and, indeed, be largely composed of) a variety of different kinds of relationships with others and move between them without confusion, the subject in a mode of relationship is always the abstraction, a persona, a person in respect of being related to others in terms of distinct and exclusive conditions. And the 'rule of law', standing for a mode of relationship, identifies a persona related to others of the same modal character.

Secondly, in spite of their modal diversity, all human relationships have a common character. Human beings are intelligent agents and the terms of all or any of the relationships they enjoy are beliefs and recognitions... Practice precedes the reflection in which its modal character is formulated.

questions.question: "Let knowledge grow from more to more But more of reverence in us dwell" In which poem of Tennyson do we find the above quoted lines?
questions.explanation: These lines come from the Prologue of Alfred, Lord Tennyson's elegy 'In Memoriam A.H.H.' (1850).

questions.question: Who is the most furious character in Fagin's Den in Dickens' Oliver Twist?
questions.explanation: Bill Sikes is the brutally violent and ferocious housebreaker and thief associated with Fagin's gang in Charles Dickens' 'Oliver Twist'.

questions.question: What can be the best explanation for the character of John Falstaff in Shakespeare's Henry IV?
questions.explanation: Sir John Falstaff is widely celebrated by literary critics (including Maurice Morgann and A. C. Bradley) as one of Shakespeare's most multifaceted and psychologically complex comic creations.

questions.question: In which play of Shakespeare do the characters 'Voltemand' and 'Cornelius' appear?
questions.explanation: Voltemand and Cornelius are Danish courtiers dispatched by King Claudius as ambassadors to Norway in Act I of Shakespeare's 'Hamlet'.

questions.question: Keats' poetry is "abundantly and enchantingly sensuous". Who has made this comment about the poetry of Keats?
questions.explanation: Matthew Arnold wrote this about Keats in his critical essay on the poet.

questions.question: "No nightingale did ever chaunt / More welcome notes to weary bands / Of travellers in some shady haunt / Among Arabian sands" Wherefrom the above quoted lines of Wordsworth are taken?
questions.explanation: These lyrical lines form the second stanza of William Wordsworth's celebrated poem 'The Solitary Reaper' (composed 1805, published 1807).

questions.question: In which famous poem does Walt Whitman make a reference to Suez Canal and wire line across the Atlantic?
questions.explanation: In 'Passage to India' (1871), Whitman celebrates three great modern engineering triumphs: the Suez Canal, the Union Pacific Transcontinental Railroad, and the Atlantic telegraph cable.

questions.question: Which of the following is the first poem of Eliot's first published volume of verse?
options: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
questions.explanation: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' was the opening poem in T. S. Eliot's landmark first poetry collection, 'Prufrock and Other Observations' (1917).

questions.question: The term 'essay' is the derivative of the French root 'essai', which means:
questions.explanation: The term originates from the French infinitive 'essayer' (meaning to attempt, trial, or try), first applied to literature by Michel de Montaigne in 1580.

questions.question: Matthew Arnold's Rugby Chapel commemorates :
questions.explanation: 'Rugby Chapel' is Matthew Arnold's elegy for his father, Dr. Thomas Arnold, the famous headmaster of Rugby School.

questions.question: Who has written the essay, 'The Old Benchers of the Inner Temple' ?
questions.explanation: 'The Old Benchers of the Inner Temple' is one of the nostalgic personal essays published in Charles Lamb's 'Essays of Elia' (1823).

questions.question: Ernest Hemingway's Men at War is:
questions.explanation: 'Men at War: The Best War Stories of All Time' (1942) is an anthology of war literature and stories edited with an extensive introduction by Ernest Hemingway.

questions.question: "The analogy was that of the catalyst. When the two gases, previously mentioned, are mixed in the presence of a filament of platinum, they form sulphurous acid... The mind of the poet is the shred of platinum." The above lines are an extract from T. S. Eliot's essay:
questions.explanation: This famous platinum catalyst analogy appears in Part II of T. S. Eliot's seminal critical essay 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919) to elucidate his Impersonal Theory of Poetry.

questions.question: Point out the figure of speech in the following line: "The ploughman homeward plods his weary way."
questions.explanation: In Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard', the adjective 'weary' logically belongs to the ploughman but is transferred to the 'way' (Transferred Epithet / Hypallage).

questions.question: To which character in Shakespeare's 'Hamlet' does the following description apply? "the tedious wiseacre who meddles his way to his doom"
questions.explanation: Polonius, the Lord Chamberlain of Claudius's court, is a verbose, meddlesome old counsellor who eavesdrops behind the arras and is accidentally slain by Hamlet.

questions.question: Who wrote Sohrab and Rustum?
questions.explanation: 'Sohrab and Rustum' (1853) is a celebrated narrative poem in blank verse by Matthew Arnold, drawn from the Persian epic 'Shahnameh' by Ferdowsi.

questions.question: Who praised Shakespeare thus ? "Others abide our question thou art free We ask and ask-Thou smilest and art still"
questions.explanation: These are the memorable opening lines of Matthew Arnold's sonnet entitled 'Shakespeare' (published in 1849).

questions.question: Who is 'Thyrsis' in the poem of the same name?
questions.explanation: In Matthew Arnold's pastoral elegy 'Thyrsis' (1865), the titular shepherd Thyrsis represents his dear friend and fellow poet Arthur Hugh Clough.

questions.question: Which of the following novels of Dickens was left unfinished ?
questions.explanation: Charles Dickens had only completed six of the planned twelve monthly installments of 'The Mystery of Edwin Drood' when he suffered a fatal stroke in June 1870.

questions.question: Nissim Ezekiel's poem, 'Background, Casually' reflects :
questions.explanation: The autobiographical poem explores Ezekiel's cultural displacement, alienation, and marginal identity as a Bene-Israel Jew growing up in multi-religious Mumbai.

questions.question: Point out the figure of speech in the following: "Little sorrows sit and weep"
questions.explanation: The abstract noun 'sorrows' is given human actions (sitting and weeping), which is a clear instance of Personification.

questions.question: Frederick Henry, the hero of Hemingway's novel, A Farewell to Arms, is a driver in :
questions.explanation: Lieutenant Frederic Henry is an American expatriate serving as an ambulance driver in the volunteer ambulance corps of the Italian Army.

questions.question: Who is the author of The Unvanquished?
questions.explanation: 'The Unvanquished' (1938) is an American Civil War novel by Nobel laureate William Faulkner revolving around the Sartoris family.

questions.question: Santiago is the hero of Hemingway's novel :
options: The Old Man and the Sea
questions.explanation: Santiago is the resilient old Cuban fisherman who battles a giant marlin and predatory sharks in 'The Old Man and the Sea' (1952).

questions.question: What was the origin of the race of Nissim Ezekiel ?
questions.explanation: Nissim Ezekiel was born into Mumbai's ancient Bene Israel Jewish community, which had settled on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra centuries earlier.

questions.question: In which year did Robert Frost sell his farm in New England and moved to England?
questions.explanation: Robert Frost sailed with his family to England in August 1912. Sources differ on whether the Derry farm was sold in 1911 or 1912; the answer counted here is 1912.

questions.question: Who has called Shelley a 'perfect singing God' ?
questions.explanation: Swinburne called Shelley 'the perfect singing-god' in his essay on Shelley in 'Essays and Studies' (1875).

questions.question: Munoo' is the central character of M. R. Anand's novel :
questions.explanation: Munoo, an innocent hill boy from Kangra whose life is cut short by brutal capitalist and imperial exploitation, is the protagonist of Mulk Raj Anand's 'Coolie' (1936).

questions.question: Who said, "The poet is a man speaking to men"?
questions.explanation: William Wordsworth made this classic democratic definition of the poet in his 'Preface to Lyrical Ballads' (1800/1802).

questions.question: The romantic poetry is a revival of :
questions.explanation: Romantic poetry is profoundly characterized by the revival of medieval romance, chivalric themes, ballads, gothic wonder, and supernatural mystery.

questions.question: The Dance of Eunuchs has been written by:
questions.explanation: 'The Dance of the Eunuchs' is a powerful, impassioned opening poem in Kamala Das's maiden collection 'Summer in Calcutta' (1965).

questions.question: How many times did Robert Frost win the prestigious Pulitzer Prize?
questions.explanation: Robert Frost remains the only poet in history to win the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry four times: in 1924, 1931, 1937, and 1943.

questions.question: "The rest is silence"-These are the last words of ________ before his death in Shakespeare.
questions.explanation: Prince Hamlet utters 'The rest is silence' to his loyal friend Horatio right before dying in Act V, Scene 2 of 'Hamlet'.

questions.question: The 'iambic pentameter' implies which of the following ?
options: Five syllables in the pattern unstressed-stressed
Five syllables in the pattern stressed-unstressed
The pattern stressed-unstressed repeated five times
The pattern unstressed-stressed repeated five times
questions.explanation: An iamb is a metrical foot consisting of one unstressed syllable followed by one stressed syllable (da-DUM); pentameter means this pattern repeats five times per line (ten syllables total).

questions.question: Which work was left incomplete because of Hemingway's sudden death?
questions.explanation: Hemingway died in 1961 and left more than one work unfinished. This test counts 'The Garden of Eden', which he worked on from 1946 until his death and which was published in 1986 in a shortened form.
questions.note: Hemingway left more than one work unfinished. This site counts one of them.

questions.question: The rhetorical device of 'anaphora' implies which of the following?
options: A certain metrical arrangement in lines
Juxtaposing the abstract with the concrete
Repeating the first word or words of successive sentences or clauses
questions.explanation: Anaphora is a rhetorical figure that consists of repeating a sequence of words at the beginnings of neighboring clauses or sentences.

questions.question: Which of the following works is not associated with Matthew Arnold?
questions.explanation: 'Culture and Environment' (1933) was written by F. R. Leavis and Denys Thompson. Matthew Arnold wrote 'Culture and Anarchy' (1869).

questions.question: The Waste Land was first published in the year:
questions.explanation: T. S. Eliot's landmark modernist poem 'The Waste Land' was first published in October 1922 in his own quarterly journal 'The Criterion' and in America in 'The Dial'.

questions.question: The Lake District in England is associated with:
questions.explanation: William Wordsworth, along with Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Robert Southey, lived in Cumbria's picturesque Lake District and became renowned as the 'Lake Poets'.

questions.question: Essays of Elia is:
options: remarkable for their terse and aphoristic style
questions.explanation: Charles Lamb's essays under the pseudonym 'Elia' are quintessentially personal, lyric, intimate, and steeped in charming autobiographical reminiscences of his youth, relatives, and workplaces.

questions.question: Milton's Samson Agonistes is:
questions.explanation: 'Samson Agonistes' (1671) is John Milton's tragic closet drama composed strictly on the model of classical Greek tragedy (Aristotelian unities, Chorus, messenger).

questions.question: "Good fences make good neighbours" This line occurs in which poem of Frost ?
questions.explanation: This traditional New England adage is repeated by the speaker's tradition-bound neighbor in Robert Frost's poem 'Mending Wall' (1914).

questions.question: Which of the following is a work of Ezekiel?
questions.explanation: 'A Time to Change' (1952), published in London by Fortune Press, was Nissim Ezekiel's groundbreaking debut collection of poems.

questions.question: The name of Macbeth's wife in the Shakespearean play is :
questions.explanation: In Shakespeare's tragedy, she is simply referred to as 'Lady Macbeth' throughout the script; historically, her name was Gruoch.

questions.question: The figure of speech used in the following sentence is: "All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand."
questions.explanation: Lady Macbeth's anguished statement in the sleepwalking scene (Act V, Scene 1) is a classic example of Hyperbole (deliberate dramatic overstatement).

questions.question: Who first imported sonnet to England ?
questions.explanation: Sir Thomas Wyatt translated Petrarchan sonnets into English during the reign of King Henry VIII, introducing the 14-line sonnet form to England.

questions.question: Which one of the following theatre companies was owned by Shakespeare where his masterpieces were first performed?
questions.explanation: The Globe Theatre in London was built in 1599 by Shakespeare's playing company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men (in which Shakespeare was a shareholder and principal playwright).

questions.question: "To follow knowledge like a sinking star Beyond the utmost bound of human thought." Who wrote these lines?
questions.explanation: These stirring lines are spoken by the aged Greek hero Ulysses in Alfred, Lord Tennyson's dramatic monologue 'Ulysses' (1842).

questions.question: "O God! O God! How weary, stale and unprofitable Seems to me all the uses of this world!" Which of Shakespeare's tragic heroes utters these words?
questions.explanation: Prince Hamlet utters these despondent words in his very first soliloquy (Act I, Scene 2) after his mother's hasty marriage to Claudius.

questions.question: Which of the following novels of Hemingway deals with his actual disappointing experiences of love and war?
options: Across the River and into the Trees
questions.explanation: 'A Farewell to Arms' (1929) draws heavily on Hemingway's real-life WWI ambulance service in Italy and his painful romance with Red Cross nurse Agnes von Kurowsky.

questions.question: In Yeats' poem Sailing to Byzantium, 'Byzantium' refers to :
questions.explanation: Byzantium was the ancient Greek colony later renamed Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul), symbolizing in Yeats' mythology the timeless golden city of intellect, art, and spirit.

questions.question: Tennyson's poetry represents :
options: Victorian spirit of questioning and loss of faith
questions.explanation: Tennyson's poetry mirrors the quintessential 'Victorian Compromise' between science and religion, progress and tradition, faith and scientific doubt.

questions.question: Who coined the phrase "Poetry is the criticism of life"?
questions.explanation: Matthew Arnold famously coined this enduring definition of literature in 'The Study of Poetry' (1880).

questions.question: Philip Pirrip' is a character in Charles Dickens' novel :
questions.explanation: Philip Pirrip, universally known as 'Pip', is the narrator and central character of Dickens' 'Great Expectations' (1861).

questions.question: Who wrote the poem The Triumph of Life?
questions.explanation: 'The Triumph of Life' (composed in 1822) was P. B. Shelley's visionary allegorical poem in terza rima, unfinished at his death.

questions.question: The word 'furtive' means:
questions.explanation: 'Furtive' means attempting to avoid notice or attention, typically because of guilt; secretive, stealthy, or surreptitious.

questions.question: Find out the correct meaning of 'stimulate':
questions.explanation: To 'stimulate' means to raise levels of physiological or nervous activity; to encourage, excite, or rouse interest and action.

questions.question: PERPETUAL means:
questions.explanation: 'Perpetual' means never ending or changing; occurring repeatedly; everlasting, continuous, or eternal.

questions.question: The word 'disparity' means:
questions.explanation: 'Disparity' denotes a noticeable and often unfair difference, imbalance, or inequality between things or people.

questions.question: Chronicle plays were very popular in :
questions.explanation: Chronicle or English history plays (based on Holinshed and Hall) reached the peak of immense nationalistic popularity in Elizabethan England in the late 16th century (1590s).

questions.question: 'Lyrical Ballads' was first published in :
questions.explanation: 'Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems' by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge was published in 1798. It is taken as the start of the English Romantic movement.

questions.question: A long romance entitled Endymion is written by:
questions.explanation: John Keats composed his 4,000-line pastoral poetic romance 'Endymion' in heroic couplets in 1818, based on the Greek myth of the shepherd loved by the Moon goddess Cynthia.

questions.question: Robert Browning is famous for his :
questions.explanation: Robert Browning brought the dramatic monologue form to its highest artistic and psychological perfection in masterpieces like 'My Last Duchess', 'Fra Lippo Lippi', and 'Andrea del Sarto'.

questions.question: T. S. Eliot declared himself to be a :
questions.explanation: In the preface to 'For Lancelot Andrewes' (1928), T. S. Eliot famously proclaimed himself 'classicist in literature, royalist in politics, and anglo-catholic in religion'.

questions.question: Who said, "Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion but an escape from emotion" ?
questions.explanation: This central tenet of the Impersonal Theory of Poetry appears in T. S. Eliot's essay 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919).

questions.question: The phrase 'stream of consciousness' was first used by:
questions.explanation: American philosopher and psychologist William James coined the term 'stream of consciousness' in his seminal book 'The Principles of Psychology' (1890).

questions.question: In which poem does Tennyson commemorate his friend 'Arthur Hallam' ?
questions.explanation: Tennyson spent nearly two decades writing 'In Memoriam A.H.H.' (1850) following the sudden death of his Cambridge friend Arthur Henry Hallam in Vienna in 1833.

questions.question: In which poem has Wordsworth described different moods of nature?
questions.explanation: In 'Tintern Abbey' (1798), Wordsworth traces his evolving psychological and spiritual relationship with Nature through different stages: animal passion, sensory delight, and mature spiritual communion.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an essay by Charles Lamb?
questions.explanation: 'On Going a Journey' (1822) is one of William Hazlitt's most celebrated essays from 'Table-Talk'; the other three are famous essays by Charles Lamb in 'Essays of Elia'.

questions.question: The idiom 'double Dutch' means:
questions.explanation: In English idiom, 'double Dutch' denotes speech or writing that is entirely incomprehensible, confusing, or gibberish.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of the following idiom: 'in cold blood'
questions.explanation: To do something 'in cold blood' means ruthlessly, dispassionately, without emotion, and with deliberate premeditation.

questions.question: What does the underlined expression mean? "Every verdict that he gave was sui generis."
questions.explanation: 'Sui generis' is a Latin legal and literary term meaning 'of its own kind', constituting a class of its own; hence, completely unique or singular.

questions.question: That which stays for a long time is:
questions.explanation: 'Durable' refers to an object or material able to withstand wear, pressure, or damage and remain functional over a long period.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'Penelope's web' mean?
questions.explanation: From Homer's Odyssey, Penelope promised to choose a suitor once she finished weaving a shroud, which she unpicked each night; thus 'Penelope's web' means an endless or futile task that is never completed.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the idiom 'ins and outs' ?
questions.explanation: The 'ins and outs' of something refers to all its intricate details, complex aspects, and inner workings.

questions.question: The antonym of GENUINE is :
questions.explanation: 'Genuine' means authentic, true, or real; its direct antonym is 'spurious' (counterfeit, fake, or false).

questions.question: The antonym of VOLUNTEER is :
questions.explanation: A 'volunteer' enters service by free choice; a 'conscript' is enrolled into military or other service compulsorily by government order.

questions.question: The antonym of AGILE is:
questions.explanation: 'Agile' means able to move quickly and easily; its opposite among the options is 'slow' (sluggish/uncoordinated).

questions.question: Give the correct antonym of the word 'prodigal'.
questions.explanation: 'Prodigal' means wasteful, recklessly extravagant; its antonym is 'frugal' or thrifty.

questions.question: The synonym of AMNESTY is:
questions.explanation: 'Amnesty' refers to an official general pardon granted by a government for political or other offenses.

questions.question: The synonym of ADROIT is :
questions.explanation: 'Adroit' (from French à droit) means clever, adept, or dexterous in using the hands or mind; highly skilful.

questions.question: The synonym of APEX is :
questions.explanation: 'Apex' means the top or highest point of something, especially one forming a point; peak, zenith, or summit.

questions.question: The synonym of FELICITOUS is :
questions.explanation: 'Felicitous' means suited to the circumstances; apt, well-chosen, and causing happiness (from Latin felix = happy/fruitful).

questions.question: Find out the correctly spelt word from the following:
questions.explanation: 'Concupiscence' (strong sexual desire/lust) is correctly spelled. (Others: concomitant, concordant, condescension).

questions.question: Find out the correct spelling:
questions.explanation: The correct spelling of the medical term related to rheumatism is 'rheumatic'.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct spelling?
questions.explanation: The usual spelling is 'irreconcilable'. Of the four forms printed here, option (3) is the closest to it, and dictionaries list this form as an old, archaic spelling.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of the word 'peruse':
questions.explanation: 'Peruse' strictly means to read, examine, or study with care and thorough attention.

questions.question: Choose the correct word to fill in the blank: Wordsworth was a great lover of natural scenery and ________.
questions.explanation: The noun 'sight' means things that are seen, spectacles, or visual scenes ('scenery and sight').

questions.question: Choose the most appropriate one-word substitute: 'an office with good salary but no work'
questions.explanation: A 'sinecure' (from Latin sine cura = without care) is a position or office requiring little or no work but yielding financial benefit.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'black and blue'
questions.explanation: 'Black and blue' describes skin discolored by extensive bruising; figuratively, to beat or thrash someone severely ('beaten black and blue').

questions.question: Choose the most appropriate one-word substitute: 'a supporter of the cause of women'
questions.explanation: A 'feminist' is an advocate for the rights and equality of women on grounds of political, social, and economic equality.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'a room for the display of works of art'
questions.explanation: An 'art gallery' is a room, building, or exhibition space specifically designed for the public display of paintings, sculptures, and works of art.

questions.question: Select the best choice to replace the underlined expression: "Aditya was not selected for the job of a medical officer because he was wet behind the ears."
questions.explanation: The colloquial idiom 'wet behind the ears' describes someone who is naive, immature, or lacking practical experience.

questions.question: 'With a high hand' means:
questions.explanation: 'With a high hand' (high-handedly) means in an arrogant, autocratic, dictatorial, or overbearing manner.

questions.question: Which of the following means 'a charlatan'?
options: who pretends to have more skill than he really has
questions.explanation: A 'charlatan' is a quack, fraud, or imposter who falsely claims to possess special knowledge or skills (especially in medicine or law).

questions.question: The appropriate meaning of 'El Dorado' is:
questions.explanation: Originally a mythical city of gold sought by Spanish explorers, 'El Dorado' figuratively signifies a visionary, unattainable dream or place of fabulous abundance.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with appropriate word: The tree was ________ with fruits.
questions.explanation: The adjective/participle 'laden' specifically collocates with the preposition 'with' when describing trees heavily weighed down with harvest: 'laden with fruits'.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is a correct one?
options: The ship let go its anchor.
Let the ship go its anchor.
Let its anchor go the ship.
Its anchor let the ship go.
questions.explanation: In standard nautical and English usage, 'let go' functions as a transitive phrasal verb meaning to release or drop: 'The ship let go its anchor'.

questions.question: Find out the correct indirect narration: "Please, please, don't drink too much. Remember that you'll have to drive home," she said to him.
options: She forbade him not to drink too much, reminding him that he would have to drive home.
She begged him not to drink too much, reminding him that he would have to drive home.
She requested him again and again that he should not drink too much. She told him to remember that he will have to drive home.
She said to him please did not drink too much and remember that he'll have to drive home.
questions.explanation: 'Please, please' conveys intense pleading, perfectly rendered by 'begged', and the tense shifted to 'would have to drive'.

questions.question: Which of the given options is the correct indirect form of speech? "Wish you a happy journey," Neeta said to me.
options: Neeta told me that I should wish a happy journey.
Neeta wished me a happy journey.
Neeta told me to have a happy journey.
Neeta wished me that I wish a happy journey.
questions.explanation: Optative sentences expressing wishes or greetings are reported simply and concisely: Subject + wished + Indirect Object + Direct Object ('Neeta wished me a happy journey').

questions.question: Point out the correct indirect form of: The mother said, "Do not go out in rain."
options: Mother requested (him) not to go out in rain.
Mother pleaded not to go out in rain.
Mother suggested (me) not to go out in rain.
Mother forbade (her) to go out in rain.
questions.explanation: The verb 'forbade' (past of forbid) conveys a negative order prohibiting an action; it takes an infinitive with 'to' without a negative particle 'not'.

questions.question: Complete the following sentence: Please refer to the subject ________ above.
questions.explanation: 'Cited' means quoted, mentioned, or referred to as an authority or precedent ('the subject cited above').

questions.question: He jumped off the bus while it ________.
questions.explanation: An action interrupted or occurring simultaneously while another action was in continuous progress requires the Past Continuous tense ('was moving').

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is correct?
options: Full many a flowers are born to blush unseen.
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen.
Full many a flower are born to blush unseen.
Full many a flowers is born to blush unseen.
questions.explanation: The grammatical construction 'many a' is followed by a singular countable noun ('flower') and a singular verb ('is born'), as in Thomas Gray's famous Elegy.

questions.question: I am looking forward to ________.
questions.explanation: In the phrasal construction 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund ('-ing' form), hence 'seeing my friend'.

questions.question: The gardens in Srinagar are more beautiful than ________.
questions.explanation: To avoid repetition when comparing plural nouns ('The gardens'), the demonstrative pronoun 'those' is used: 'more beautiful than those in Mysore'.

questions.question: My friend came all the way from Kathmandu to congratulate me ________ my success.
questions.explanation: The verb 'congratulate' takes the fixed preposition 'on' followed by the achievement: 'congratulate someone ON something'.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is correct one ?
options: I went there with a view to meet him.
I went there with a view to meeting him.
I went there for a view to meeting him.
I went there with views to meeting him.
questions.explanation: The fixed prepositional phrase 'with a view to' requires a gerund ('-ing' verb form), yielding 'with a view to meeting him'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with appropriate tense: I wish I ________ dead.
questions.explanation: In expressions of an unreal, hypothetical, or impossible present wish after 'I wish', the subjunctive mood uses the plural past form 'were' for all persons.

questions.question: In a state or society human beings are associated with one another in terms of :
questions.explanation: The opening sentence of the comprehension passage clearly states: 'The expression 'the rule of law' relates to human association... associated in terms of the recognition of certain conditions of association, namely 'laws''.

questions.question: In the context of the passage, which of the following statements is not correct?
options: All human relationships are based on laws.
There are different modes of relationships among human beings.
Legal relationships can be indisputably blended with non-legal relationships.
There is no contradiction between a civil and an ecclesiastical relationship.
questions.explanation: The passage says that people have many different kinds of relationships and move between them. So it is not true that all human relationships are based on laws.

questions.question: Throughout the passage, the term 'mode' implies:
questions.explanation: In philosophical discourse, 'mode of association' denotes a distinct form, structure, or category of relationship.

questions.question: In the phrase 'contingent assemblages', contingent means :
questions.explanation: 'Contingent' in philosophical terminology means non-necessary, dependent on circumstance, or incidental/accidental.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about 'the rule of law' ?
options: In spite of difference, human beings can accept the same modal character.
Human beings cannot be subjected to the same 'rule of law'.
All men and women being alike, the same 'rule of law' is not difficult to endorse.
Human beings are too egoistical to accept a common 'rule of law'.
questions.explanation: The passage says the 'rule of law' identifies a persona related to others of the same modal character, in spite of the differences between them.

questions.question: The tone of the passage is:
questions.explanation: The author systematically sets out, explains, and analyzes the theoretical conditions of human relationships and the rule of law, which is an expository tone.

questions.question: Mark the part containing an error: Every one of us (1) / should do our duty (2) / to the country. (3) / No error (4)
questions.explanation: 'Every one of us' goes with 'our'. The pronoun agrees with 'us', so the sentence has no error.

questions.question: Mark the part containing an error: Very few people now (1) / believe that (2) / the wages of sin are (3) / death. (4)
questions.explanation: In the biblical proverb (Romans 6:23), 'wages' when meaning retribution or consequence takes a singular verb: 'The wages of sin IS death'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with correct preposition: I do not agree ________ your proposal.
questions.explanation: Idiomatic preposition usage: one 'agrees WITH a person' on an issue, but 'agrees TO a proposal, plan, or suggestion'.

questions.question: Choose the correct tense of verb: I waited for my friend until he ________.
questions.explanation: The main clause verb 'waited' is in the simple past tense, requiring the simple past 'came' after the temporal conjunction 'until'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Silkworm feed ________ mulberry trees.
questions.explanation: Animals and insects 'feed ON' their food or plants ('Silkworms feed on mulberry leaves/trees').

questions.question: Choose the correct transformation from complex to simple: "While there is life, there is hope."
options: So long as there is life, there is hope.
Until there is hope, there is life.
Where the life is, the hope is there.
questions.explanation: A simple sentence contains only one finite verb and no subordinate clause; option (2) eliminates the subordinate clause 'while...' by transforming it into a single independent clause with a compound subject.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct preposition : The cat is hiding ________ us.
questions.explanation: One hides 'FROM' someone or something to avoid being seen or found ('hiding from us').
